questions.stem: A 28-year-old man plans to fly from sea level to a high-altitude ski resort and reports that on a previous trip he developed headache, nausea, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath the day after arrival. His physician prescribes a drug whose generic name ends in "-zolamide" to take prior to ascent. By inhibiting which enzyme does this drug work?
explanations: Correct. Drugs ending in "-zolamide" (e.g., acetazolamide) are carbonic anhydrase inhibitors that block the enzyme catalyzing CO2 + H2O ↔ HCO3− + H+.
Incorrect. Cyclooxygenase is targeted by NSAIDs, not by carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
Incorrect. Cardiac glycosides like digoxin block Na+/K+-ATPase; CAIs do not.
Incorrect. Phosphodiesterase inhibitors include drugs like sildenafil; this is unrelated to CAI mechanism.
Incorrect. Xanthine oxidase is inhibited by allopurinol, not by CAIs.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma is started on oral acetazolamide. Which reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme that this drug inhibits?
explanations: Incorrect. cAMP synthesis is catalyzed by adenylyl cyclase, not carbonic anhydrase.
Correct. Carbonic anhydrase reversibly catalyzes the conversion of CO2 and water into bicarbonate and protons (the carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffer system).
Incorrect. This is the hexokinase reaction.
Incorrect. This is the lactate dehydrogenase reaction.
Incorrect. This reaction is catalyzed by xanthine oxidase.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is started on acetazolamide for idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The drug is most active in which segment of the nephron, where it produces its diuretic effect?
explanations: Incorrect. K+-sparing diuretics act in the collecting duct, not CAIs.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics act on the thick ascending limb of Henle.
Incorrect. Thiazide diuretics act on the distal convoluted tubule.
Correct. CAIs are most active in the proximal tubule, where carbonic anhydrase is required for filtered bicarbonate reabsorption.
Incorrect. The thin descending limb is permeable to water but is not a primary site of diuretic action.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is given acetazolamide. In the proximal tubule, the bicarbonate reabsorption process that this drug interrupts is inevitably linked to reabsorption of which other ion via an antiporter on the apical membrane?
explanations: Incorrect. Calcium reabsorption is not coupled to bicarbonate reabsorption via this antiporter.
Incorrect. The antiporter that drives bicarbonate reabsorption exchanges Na+ for H+, not chloride.
Incorrect. Magnesium is reabsorbed primarily in the thick ascending limb, not via the proximal Na+/H+ antiporter.
Incorrect. Potassium is excreted along with bicarbonate when CAIs are given; it is not the antiported partner.
Correct. HCO3− reabsorption is inevitably linked to Na+ reabsorption via the apical Na+/H+ antiporter that pumps Na+ in and H+ out.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man takes acetazolamide for several days and develops a non–anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Which acid–base disorder does this drug characteristically induce, and by what renal mechanism?
choices: Metabolic acidosis from impaired HCO3− reabsorption
Metabolic acidosis from organic acid generation
Metabolic alkalosis from urinary H+ loss
explanations: Correct. CAIs cause a drug-induced proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis because the tubule can no longer reabsorb filtered HCO3−.
Incorrect. CAIs do not cause acidosis by generating organic acids; the mechanism is loss of bicarbonate.
Incorrect. CAIs cause acidosis, not alkalosis.
Incorrect. CAIs do not impair pulmonary CO2 excretion; in fact they lead to compensatory hyperventilation.
Incorrect. The primary disturbance is metabolic acidosis; any hyperventilation is compensatory rather than a direct CNS effect.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old climber takes acetazolamide several days before ascending to high altitude. Which sequence best explains how this drug prevents altitude sickness?
explanations: Correct. By blocking renal CA, acetazolamide increases urinary bicarbonate excretion, producing metabolic acidosis that drives compensatory hyperventilation, raising arterial oxygen and preventing altitude sickness.
Incorrect. CAIs cause metabolic acidosis (not alkalosis) and stimulate, rather than suppress, ventilation.
Incorrect. The mechanism is acid–base, not volume- or erythropoietin-mediated.
Incorrect. CAIs increase, not decrease, urinary HCO3− and do not cause respiratory acidosis.
Incorrect. CAIs cause hypokalemia from K+ being excreted with bicarbonate, not hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic open-angle glaucoma is started on a topical CAI eye drop to lower his intraocular pressure. Which structure in the eye produces the fluid that this drug targets?
explanations: Incorrect. The canal of Schlemm provides outflow drainage for aqueous humor; it does not produce it.
Incorrect. The choroid plexus produces CSF, not aqueous humor.
Correct. The ciliary body in the posterior chamber produces aqueous humor, a hyperosmotic solution composed primarily of Na+ and HCO3−.
Incorrect. The lens does not produce aqueous humor.
Incorrect. The trabecular meshwork is the site of aqueous humor resorption, not production.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is being managed for open-angle glaucoma. By which mechanism do CAIs lower intraocular pressure?
choices: Decreasing ciliary HCO3− and aqueous humor
Inhibiting α1 receptors on the iris
explanations: Incorrect. CAIs do not act on the pupil or iris musculature.
Correct. CAIs decrease HCO3− production by the ciliary body, which reduces aqueous humor formation and thereby lowers intraocular pressure.
Incorrect. CAIs reduce production of aqueous humor; they do not increase outflow through Schlemm.
Incorrect. CAIs inhibit carbonic anhydrase, not adrenergic receptors.
Incorrect. CAIs are not prostaglandin inhibitors; that is the mechanism of NSAIDs.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old obese woman with daily headaches and papilledema is diagnosed with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri). She is started on acetazolamide. Which mechanism best explains the drug's benefit in this condition?
choices: Decreased CSF production by choroid plexus
explanations: Incorrect. CAIs lower ICP by reducing CSF production, not by direct cerebral vasoconstriction.
Correct. CAIs inhibit intracellular CA in the choroid plexus, reducing HCO3− and therefore CSF production, lowering ICP.
Incorrect. CAIs do not enhance arachnoid granulation reabsorption.
Incorrect. The diuretic effect of CAIs is mild and is not the principal mechanism in pseudotumor cerebri.
Incorrect. CAIs actually stimulate ventilation by causing acidosis; they do not inhibit chemoreceptors.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with poorly controlled epilepsy is given a drug that ends in "-zolamide" as add-on therapy for refractory seizures. Which intracellular abnormality in some forms of epilepsy provides the rationale for using this drug?
explanations: Incorrect. The brick describes increased, not decreased, neuronal CA activity in some epilepsy.
Incorrect. Na+/K+-ATPase dysfunction is not the rationale described in the brick.
Incorrect. Epilepsy is characterized by reduced inhibition or increased excitation, not excess GABA activity.
Correct. Some epileptic neurons show increased CA activity producing high intracellular bicarbonate, which contributes to uncoordinated neuronal firing; CAIs correct this imbalance.
Incorrect. The brick does not attribute the seizure mechanism to calcium channel changes.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with COPD is being weaned from mechanical ventilation in the ICU. The intensivist orders acetazolamide. Which physiologic effect is being sought?
choices: Decreased serum HCO3− to ↑ respiratory drive
Increased serum HCO3− to buffer acidosis
explanations: Incorrect. CAIs are not bronchodilators.
Correct. In COPD, the kidneys raise serum HCO3− to compensate for chronic respiratory acidosis; CAIs decrease bicarbonate, increasing respiratory drive and helping wean off the ventilator.
Incorrect. CAIs decrease, not increase, serum bicarbonate.
Incorrect. CAIs do not affect mucus production.
Incorrect. CAIs do not stimulate erythropoietin.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man is being treated off-label with acetazolamide for central sleep apnea. By which mechanism does the drug improve his oxygenation during sleep?
explanations: Incorrect. Central sleep apnea is loss of respiratory effort, not airway obstruction; CAIs act on chemoreceptor drive.
Correct. CAIs increase urinary HCO3− excretion, lowering serum pH; this triggers central chemoreceptors, leading to hyperventilation and improved oxygenation.
Incorrect. CAIs stimulate, rather than inhibit, the response of central chemoreceptors.
Incorrect. Although CAIs lower CSF production, this is not the mechanism for improving central sleep apnea.
Incorrect. IOP effects are unrelated to central sleep apnea.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has been taking acetazolamide before mountaineering. Routine labs reveal a low serum potassium and a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Why does CAI use lead to hypokalemia?
choices: Direct block of K+ in TAL
explanations: Incorrect. The brick attributes K+ loss to its excretion with bicarbonate, not to ENaC-mediated effects.
Incorrect. CAIs do not act on Na+/K+-ATPase.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics affect the thick ascending limb; CAIs act in the proximal tubule.
Correct. Per the brick, potassium is excreted along with the bicarbonate that the renal tubule cannot reabsorb, leading to hypokalemia.
Incorrect. Acidosis tends to shift K+ out of cells, raising serum K+; this does not explain CAI-induced hypokalemia.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man on chronic acetazolamide develops right flank pain and gross hematuria. CT shows a renal calculus. Which composition is most consistent with the stones associated with CAI therapy?
explanations: Incorrect. Calcium oxalate stones are not the type specifically linked to CAI use in the brick.
Correct. Alkalinization of the urine from CAIs may lead to formation of renal calcium phosphate stones.
Incorrect. Cystine stones are caused by hereditary cystinuria, not by CAIs.
Incorrect. Struvite stones form in the setting of urease-producing bacterial infections.
Incorrect. Uric acid stones precipitate in acidic urine; CAI-induced alkaline urine actually disfavors them.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman started on acetazolamide for idiopathic intracranial hypertension reports new tingling in her fingers and toes and intermittent ringing in her ears. These adverse effects are best categorized as which class of CAI side effect?
explanations: Incorrect. The brick does not describe cardiotoxicity from CAIs.
Incorrect. The brick does not list hematologic adverse effects.
Incorrect. CAIs may worsen liver disease, but paresthesias and tinnitus are not categorized as hepatotoxic.
Incorrect. Renal stones are a separate adverse effect category.
Correct. Paresthesias (tingling in extremities) and tinnitus (ringing in the ears) are classified as neurologic side effects of CAIs.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with a history of severe rash after taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole presents with newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma. Which feature of CAIs makes them contraindicated in this patient?
explanations: Incorrect. CAIs do not contain a beta-lactam ring.
Incorrect. CAIs cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. CAIs are not macrolide-class drugs.
Correct. CAIs contain a sulfonamide group and are contraindicated in patients with a sulfa allergy.
Incorrect. Chelation with calcium is a tetracycline property, not a CAI property.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic alcohol use is found to have elevated intraocular pressure. The clinician avoids prescribing acetazolamide. What is the primary concern in this patient?
explanations: Incorrect. CAIs do not cause sodium retention; they promote sodium loss.
Incorrect. CAIs cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
Correct. CAIs should be avoided in patients with cirrhosis because they may precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.
Incorrect. CAIs do not cause volume overload or hypertension; they are mild diuretics.
Incorrect. CAIs are not used for fluid overload but they do not characteristically worsen pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman in her second trimester is diagnosed with idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Her physician discusses CAI therapy. Which best characterizes the use of CAIs in pregnancy?
explanations: Incorrect. The brick does not classify CAIs as absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
Incorrect. There are not abundant human safety data; CAIs are not category A.
Incorrect. CAIs are category C, not B, in the brick.
Correct. CAIs are category C drugs in pregnancy, to be used cautiously and only when the benefit may outweigh the risk.
Incorrect. CAIs are category C, not category X.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old hypertensive man is found to have mildly elevated intraocular pressure. His physician notes that, unlike thiazides or loop diuretics, CAIs are not first-line therapy for his hypertension. What is the principal reason CAIs are not used for fluid overload or hypertension?
explanations: Incorrect. CAIs cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia, and that is not why they are not used for hypertension.
Correct. The brick states that CAIs are not used for fluid overload or hypertension because their diuretic effect is much weaker than that of other diuretics.
Incorrect. CAIs do not cause vasoconstriction.
Incorrect. CAIs do reduce sodium reabsorption (linked to bicarbonate); the issue is potency, not lack of effect.
Incorrect. The brick does not cite renal blood flow as the limiting factor.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with chronic open-angle glaucoma is started on long-term therapy. To minimize systemic adverse effects while still treating her glaucoma, which CAI route is preferred?
explanations: Incorrect. Intramuscular dosing is not the preferred route for chronic glaucoma in the brick.
Incorrect. IV acetazolamide is reserved for systemic indications such as acute severe glaucoma.
Incorrect. Methazolamide is oral and would still produce systemic effects compared with a topical agent.
Incorrect. Subcutaneous dosing is not described.
Correct. For chronic long-term glaucoma therapy, topical CAIs (e.g., brinzolamide) are preferred because they generally avoid systemic effects.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with an acute, severe attack of open-angle glaucoma. Which CAI choice and route is most appropriate for this acute presentation?
explanations: Incorrect. Topical brinzolamide is preferred for chronic, not acute severe, glaucoma per the brick.
Incorrect. Topical dorzolamide is also chronic-therapy oriented.
Incorrect. Methazolamide is given orally, not topically.
Correct. For an acute severe case of glaucoma the brick recommends systemic therapy with acetazolamide (oral or IV).
Incorrect. Brinzolamide is administered topically, not subcutaneously.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the proximal tubule cell diagram showing bicarbonate reabsorption. In the tubular lumen, filtered HCO3− combines with secreted H+ to form H2CO3, which CA then converts to which two molecules that diffuse into the cell?
explanations: Incorrect. Ammonia is not generated by this reaction.
Correct. CA in the lumen converts H2CO3 into CO2 and water, which then diffuse into the proximal tubule cell where intracellular CA reverses the reaction.
Incorrect. Glucose and lactate are not products of CA.
Incorrect. Na+ and Cl− are not products of CA-catalyzed reactions.
Incorrect. Pyruvate is not produced by CA.

questions.stem: A patient is started on a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and provides a urine sample several days later. Compared with baseline, which urinary finding is expected?
explanations: Incorrect. CAIs increase, not decrease, urinary bicarbonate.
Correct. After taking the drug, the urine will be more alkaline than normal because of the extra bicarbonate (bicarbonaturia).
Incorrect. CAIs do not cause glucosuria.
Incorrect. CAIs increase urinary sodium loss along with bicarbonate.
Incorrect. Systemic CAIs act on the kidney; renal effects on bicarbonate and sodium occur with oral/IV agents.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man arrives at a high-altitude resort and rapidly develops headache and nausea consistent with altitude sickness. Which underlying acid–base disturbance is responsible for these symptoms in unprotected ascent?
explanations: Incorrect. The brick attributes altitude sickness to respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation, not lactic acidosis.
Incorrect. Renal HCO3− retention is the compensation, not the primary disturbance, in altitude sickness.
Incorrect. The brick explicitly describes an acid–base mechanism rather than dehydration.
Incorrect. At altitude, hypoxemia drives hyperventilation, not hypoventilation.
Correct. Hypoxemia at altitude induces hyperventilation that releases large amounts of CO2, producing respiratory alkalosis with headache and nausea.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with mild Alzheimer disease and a documented sulfa allergy is found to have elevated intraocular pressure on routine eye exam. His ophthalmologist considers prescribing dorzolamide eye drops. Which class-wide warning still applies even with a topical CAI?
explanations: Correct. All CAIs (including topical agents) contain a sulfonamide group and are contraindicated in patients with a sulfa allergy.
Incorrect. The brick does not describe direct cardiotoxicity from CAIs.
Incorrect. CAIs cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. CAI diuresis is mild and does not characteristically cause hypovolemic shock.
Incorrect. CAIs are pregnancy category C, not category X.
